slides.headline: A green suite nobody believes is worse than a red one.
slides.lede: How a test suite loses trust, what that costs, and the order to fix it in.
meta: Audience: engineers who have started re-running CI "to see if it passes"

slides.title: A flaky test is a broken test that lies
slides.sub: The failure isn't the intermittency. It's that the suite has started producing a signal people route around, and routing around a signal is a habit that generalises.

cards.p: It fails. Intermittency is a property of the bug, not a lesser category of bug.
You have decided the result is noise. Write that decision down, because right now it lives only in your head.
The suite is no longer a gate. It is a formality with a latency cost.

slides.note: The tell is behavioural, not statistical. You do not need a flake-rate dashboard to know you have a problem. You need to notice the first time someone says "just hit retry" and nobody argues.

slides.title: What each piece is really for
slides.sub: A suite does four separate jobs, and flakiness damages them in a specific order.
rows: Gone immediately — a gate you bypass is not a gate
You hear about a regression fast
Degrades · real failures hide among known-bad tests
The test says what the code promises
The expensive one, and the last to come back
slides.note: Read the right column bottom to top. That's the order you lose them in, and the order you have to earn them back.

slides.title: Five questions, and only four have answers

items.q: Does it fail on a clean checkout?
items.a: Then it is your environment, which is still a bug worth naming.
If it passes alone and fails in a suite, that is a fact about shared state.
Randomise it once; you will learn more than a week of staring teaches.
Then the test is right and the code is wrong — the good outcome, and the rarest.

items.q: How long has it been like this?

slides.kicker: The fifth has no answer on purpose. Almost nobody can say, because nobody was measuring, and that absence is the finding.

slides.title: Isolation, or the appearance of it
slides.sub: Most flakes are two tests disagreeing about something neither of them owns.

cards.h: A database that persists between tests
cards.p: Truncation between cases is not isolation. It is isolation until someone adds a test that depends on a row surviving.
Fast, invisible, and shared. import runs once; your setup runs every time.
Slower. Correct. If that trade is genuinely too expensive, measure it before deciding — the estimate is usually wrong by an order of magnitude.
A fixture that is deliberately shared and documented is fine. It is the accidental sharing that costs you afternoons.

slides.note: The question that finds these: what does this test assume already exists? Ask it out loud and the answer is often embarrassing.

slides.title: Anything that reads the clock is suspect
slides.sub: Time-dependent tests fail on the build machine, on a Monday, in a timezone nobody has, during a leap second.
rows: Wait for the condition, with a generous ceiling
The clock moves between the two lines
Timeout on the test, not the assertion
Your machine is not the build machine
Pin it, explicitly, in the test
R&D time spent re-running is still spent
Fix it, quarantine it, or delete it
slides.note: A wait is not a sleep. Polling for the thing you actually want takes the same line count and removes an entire category of failure. See waitFor in whichever framework you use — they all have one.

slides.title: Prove the test can fail
slides.sub: The most common defect in a test suite is not a flaky test. It is a test that passes unconditionally and always has.

items.a: Change the thing under test and watch the test go red. If it stays green, you have found a second bug.
Invert it. A test that passes both ways is asserting nothing, whatever its name claims.

items.q: Do it when you write it.
items.a: Retrofitting this to a suite of four hundred is a project. Doing it once per test is thirty seconds.

slides.quote: A test that has never failed has never been tested.
slides.note: This is not theory. Two tests written for this very deck's repository passed against an application that was genuinely broken, and were only caught by deliberately reintroducing the defect they claimed to cover.

slides.title: Fix in this order, not the obvious one
slides.sub: The instinct is to start with the noisiest test. The instinct is wrong.

items.a: Record which tests fail and how often. Without a baseline you cannot tell a fix from a coincidence.
Quarantined still runs and reports; it just does not block.
One cause, many symptoms — the count drops faster than anyone expects.

items.q: Then the clock, then the genuine races
items.a: , which are real bugs deserving real fixes.

slides.note: Quarantine has a half-life. A quarantine list with no expiry date is a deletion with extra steps. Put a date on it.

slides.title: Two numbers worth watching
slides.sub: Not a dashboard. Two numbers, reviewed when someone remembers.

cards.h: Runs since the last unexplained failure
cards.p:
Counts up. Resets to zero when something fails for a reason nobody can name.
Everyone understands it without a legend, which is most of its value.

cards.h: Time from red to a named cause
cards.p: The real measure of whether the suite is useful. A suite that fails fast and explains itself is worth more than a suite that rarely fails and never explains anything.

slides.kicker: Deliberately not a percentage. A flake rate averages away the thing you care about, which is whether this failure, today, means something.

slides.title: What to say on Monday
slides.sub: None of this needs a project, a budget, or permission.

cards.p: One flag in most runners. It will find something. Expect that, and do not treat the first red as a setback.
Which tests failed, and when. A text file is a perfectly good instrument.
Not one test. One cause. Then count how many tests stopped failing.
Pick the test you would least like to be wrong about, and prove it can fail.

slides.note: The goal is not zero failures. It is that every failure means something. A suite that goes red for a reason is doing its job.
slides.kicker: Notes, the retro that prompted this, and the raw build history are in the working notes. Corrections welcome — especially from anyone whose suite is worse than ours was.
